question: The European Commission’s recent proposal to reduce trawling days in the Mediterranean by 79 %, from an average of 130 to just 27 days per year, poses an existential threat to 556 vessels and could lead to the loss of 17 000 jobs on the Valencian-Mediterranean coast. Furthermore, the new cuts could put an end to fishermen’s guilds and lead to the privatisation of the fish markets, transforming a sustainable, local and community-based fishing model into a privatised model. In view of the above: 1.
How can the Commission justify the 79 % reduction in days at sea without putting forward additional measures to ensure the economic viability of the fleets concerned?

Has the Commission carried out a detailed socio-economic impact assessment of this measure, in particular, with regard to the threat it poses to the survival of the small-scale fishing sector, the risk of privatisation of fish markets and the potential disappearance of fishermen’s guilds in the western Mediterranean?

In view of the disparities in burden-sharing between Mediterranean and nonMediterranean regions, how does the Commission justify the compatibility of this measure with the principles of social justice and territorial cohesion?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.2.2025) The Commission proposal for the 2025 fishing opportunities under the legislative framework of the Western Mediterranean management plan1 (MAP) is based on the best available scientific advice provided by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries2 (STECF).

The advice showed that several of the stocks concerned by the MAP are outside of safe biological limits and important catch reductions are needed for the stocks to recover. The MAP’s aim is to secure a sustainable and profitable future for the sector relying on healthy fish stocks.

While the fishing opportunities adopted by the Council have gradually reduced the trawling effort since 2020, numerous flexibilities alleviated the total reduction, such as the recovered fishing days granted by the compensation mechanism. European financial assistance is available to those fishers who opt in.

For 2025, the Council adopted the fishing effort reductions proposed by Commission, together with an expanded compensation mechanism based on conservation measures. The Commission will continue working with the Member States and the fishing sector for the implementation of the MAP.

The socio-economic specificities of the Western Mediterranean fisheries were considered during the negotiations of the MAP, and the co-legislators agreed to postpone the binding rule for Maximum Sustainable Yield to 20253. The Commission has worked based on STECF socio-economic analyses that conclude how ambitious management measures will rapidly pay off with more healthy stocks and increased sector profitability.
The Commission worked with all stakeholders to implement gradually the MAP and has continuously recommended a broad range of measures4 to help with its implementation.
1 Regulation (EU) 2019/1022 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 establishing a

multiannual plan for the fisheries exploiting demersal stocks in the western Mediterranean Sea and amending Regulation (EU) No 508/2014. OJ L 172, 26.6.2019, p. 1–17. 2 STECF Expert Working Group EWG 24-10 (https://stecf.jrc.ec.europa.eu/documents/d/stecf/tors_ewg_24-10) and STECF Expert Working Group EWG 24-12 (https://stecf.jrc.ec.europa.eu/documents/d/stecf/ewg_2412_tor_westmed_fisheries-management).

3 A 5-year derogation compared to other sea basins, for which the legal requirement to achieve sustainable fisheries had to be achieved by 2020 at the latest. 4 Measures supported by the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF).
